# The Denominator

The *Vantage* has eight years of fuel left, and the people aboard cannot agree on where it should burn. Ninety-six years after the beam that launched them fell silent, a ship-born majority wants to keep its course for the world their ancestors chose from decades-old starlight; a smaller faction wants to divert toward a planet that looks wetter, more recently. The law is exact about who gets a say — and it says the 1,180 frozen founders count toward the total whether or not they ever wake to cast a vote. So before the ship can debate its destination, it must debate whether to open the vaults at all, knowing that revival is one-way and that not everyone survives it.

Juno Katsaros will run that vote and then disqualify herself from it, by the same rule she enforces on everyone else. Hanne Vollmer, who has kept the sleepers' record complete for sixteen years, has kept one page of it to herself. Oksana Brill counts water rations for a living and trusts nothing she cannot count herself. Around them: fifty days of testimony read aloud from the dead, a hall of hand-counted paper, and a warming clock on the first berths brought back — ticking down toward an answer the reader will get, and a cost the ship will not admit until it must.

Comparable to *The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet*, *Aurora*, and *Seveneves*.
# Chapter 1 — Six Hundred and Eleven

Berth 1180 had written eleven lines. Noor Sandoval read them at the pace she had held for fifty days, because a testament read fast is a testament summarised, and she did not summarise.

Her voice had gone on day thirty-one and come back wrong. The reading floor was hull deck, 0.82 g, cold enough that the mineral wool sweated. Her water ration for the day sat beside the lectern in its metered cup, and she had not touched it, because touching it meant stopping.

She finished. She turned the paper over and read the running count aloud from her own hand.

"Of one thousand one hundred and eighty testaments, six hundred and eleven contain a best-available-data clause. They instruct this ship to use the sky it can actually see, and not the spectra of the 2190s."

Twelve people. On day 154 there had been hundreds.

Hanne Vollmer went on polishing the vault door, the weekly cloth going panel to panel, and did not contest the number. "Five hundred and sixty-nine say the opposite," she said. "The Trust has quoted those for two hundred years. A guild whose whole claim is fidelity cannot be the mouth that announces the founders already let go."

Someone behind her said *the frozen*.

"Signatories," Vollmer said, and kept counting panels.

Oksana Brill came off the stairs without raising her voice. "Article 9 counts votes. Three thousand five hundred and twenty-seven of five thousand two hundred and ninety. A testament is not a chit, and a frozen signatory cannot cut one." She looked at the thin audience. "Ivers, deck 9, four litres. Sunna, deck 14, three point five. Ottoline, deck 22, four." No list. She had never needed one.

Teo Marchetti spoke from her own deck. "One hundred and ninety berths. Four thousand one hundred and ten awake plus one hundred and ninety is four thousand three hundred exactly, which the loop sustains. The biomass reserve is never opened."

"Day sixty-one," Brill said. "A betrayal from my own deck."

Evening, and Ansel Duong came down from the Long Ear with a fragment nobody had asked for, logged that day, at least 11.9 years old.

"It speaks of the beam consortium in the past tense. It calls the *Vantage* the first of three. The other two were never built." He waited. "The Epsilon Eridani water spectra came from that same source. If anyone wants to ask Sol which of these is still true, the round trip is 23.8 years."

At the eighth hour word came down the stairs that the counting hall had been cleared for day 210, and the twelve went up to see it.

Sandoval filed berth 1180 and found she had read one thousand one hundred and eighty promises to an empty floor.
# Chapter 2 — Seventy-Four

The hall opened at seventh bell with Juno Katsaros reading her own disqualification aloud, because the Charter required it and because she liked the sound of a rule that cost her something.

"Helm officers are struck from the roll while serving. I do not vote. Say it back."

The witnesses said it back. Forty of them, one from every deck, standing at the long tables under lights scheduled for the occasion. No terminal in the room was powered. Since Year 96 the ship's computers could model this to four decimals and were forbidden to touch a single chit, and Katsaros had always thought that was the most civilised sentence in the Charter.

The chits came up from the boxes in paper handfuls, still smelling of the press. Two questions each: Wake or Keep Sealed; and if Wake, Limited or Full. She counted aloud in blocks of fifty. The hall repeated each block. It took nine hours and it was, she thought, the least frightening nine hours she had spent in a year.

Twice the tables were challenged. Oksana Brill's witness objected to a chit creased across the fold; Katsaros admitted it, the mark being legible. An hour later Noor Sandoval's witness objected to a chit creased identically; Katsaros admitted that one too, on the same grounds, and neither faction thanked her. Good. Indifference was the only thing she was permitted to own in public.

What she was not permitted to own stood behind her sternum all day, cold and numbered, and said: *wake them.* She did not spend it. There was nowhere to spend it.

Idris Falk stood at the back with the ledger open on his forearm and said, to nobody, that each revival was nineteen megawatt-hours and forty days of a technician's attention, that nine in a hundred failed irreversibly, that the ship held 41.2 kilometres per second and a diversion would spend 8.7 of it before flight year 292 day 1. He offered no metaphor. He looked at her once, a half-second too long, and went back to his kilograms.

At the twenty-third hour she read the result and made them give it back to her.

"Chits cast, three thousand four hundred and ten of three thousand seven hundred and forty-eight. Wake, one thousand seven hundred and forty-two. Keep Sealed, one thousand six hundred and sixty-eight. Margin, seventy-four. Of the wake chits: Limited, one thousand four hundred and forty-one. Full, three hundred and one."

The hall gave it back. She sealed the doors herself. No recount.

Afterwards Falk waited by the empty tables. "You could say it now."

"No," said Juno Katsaros, "I couldn't," and signed the certificate in a clean hand.
# Chapter 3 — The Denominator

The door took wax the way it always had, in small circles, sixteen years of Thursdays in her wrist. Hanne Vollmer polished while the warming clock on berth 0901 ran down its last hour. Behind her the sunward deck hummed at 0.82 g and smelled of cold metal and chlorophyll, and beyond the hull the *Vantage* went on at 0.0341c toward Tau Ceti, as she had since 2211.

Flight year 209: nine days of rewarming on a failed power bus, logged as a thermal excursion, never tested. Flight year 271: sixty-four trickle signatures that did not match the other 1,116, sealed inside the only complete enrollment record aboard, which was hers. She had never been able to test them. The only test was a forty-day warming that could not be undone. In flight year 262 she had signed a death on warming day 31 with her own hand, and after that the nine percent was not a statistic to her. So she had waited for a ballot. On day 210 the ship gave her one by seventy-four chits, and chose the limited thaw — Teo Marchetti's 190 berths, the exact number the loop could absorb.

0901 opened at the scheduled minute. The technicians worked the procedure they had rehearsed for fifty years without performing it once: drain, lavage, sternal leads, the checklist read aloud. The body was warm. Nothing else about it was.

"Note the time," Vollmer said. "Signatory. Not remains. Signatory."

0902 came eleven minutes later, the same.

Noor Sandoval stood at the rail with her hands folded. "Berth 0901," she said. "Berth 0902." She had no other way to name them that she was willing to use.

Idris Falk arrived with the ledger and did not look at the tables. "Article 9 wants 3,527 of the chartered 5,290. The roll produces 3,748 chits. That was already 94.1 percent of everyone who could vote. Add 190 berths — sixty-four of them dead since 209, about eleven more to the nine percent — and the roll is roughly 3,863 and the bar is roughly 91.3 percent, and flight year 292 day 1 arrives regardless. Only the full thaw ever moved it. Three hundred and one people voted for that."

"Say what it is," said Oksana Brill, and then did not say anything else.

"It is mass and it is arithmetic," Falk said. "I won't call it anything grander."

Vollmer entered both deaths in the enrollment record, in ink, and wrote beneath them that the Charter's denominator had counted sixty-four corpses since flight year 209 — that every threshold the ship had ever computed had been computed against the dead.

Then she picked up the cloth. The door still needed polishing.
